sources.title: Implementation Completion and Results Report: Community Resilience to Climate and Disaster Risk Project (P112613)
sources.methodology: World Bank completion evaluation using project monitoring, beneficiary survey, site visits and economic analysis.
sources.limitations: M&E was rated modest; the 103-person survey was non-representative, and remote-site visits and COVID-19 limited field coverage.

sources.title: Community-based adaptation to climate change in villages of Western Province, Solomon Islands
sources.organization: Marine Pollution Bulletin; Britt Basel, Gillian Goby and Johanna Johnson; hosted by SPREP
sources.temporal_coverage: Community fieldwork and adaptation workshops in 2017; article published in 2020.
sources.methodology: Participatory workshops, interviews and semi-quantitative vulnerability assessment in two Rendova communities.
sources.limitations: Two purposively selected communities had existing leadership and conservation ties; not representative.

sources.title: Climate-related disasters and temperature extremes are not associated with conflict risk in Pacific Island countries
sources.organization: Environment and Security; Tobias Ide, Ore Koren and Luke Derrick
sources.temporal_coverage: Geocoded conflict and climate-event dataset for 2012-2020; article first published online 2026-01-22.
sources.methodology: Original geocoded social-conflict dataset and panel regressions at 0.5-degree cell-year scale across three Pacific countries, with contextual controls and robustness tests.
sources.limitations: The 2012-2020 panel cannot directly test causal mechanisms; few disasters and incomplete precipitation-extreme coverage limit inference, and organized armed-group conflict was outside scope.

sources.title: Community-Led Climate Adaptation Projects Strengthen Resilience Across Solomon Islands
sources.organization: United Nations Development Programme, Pacific Office
sources.temporal_coverage: Community-Based Adaptation Phase III investments 2022-2026; closing workshop in June 2026; page dated 2026-08-25.
sources.methodology: Official UNDP programme-completion announcement summarizing community project outputs and a June 2026 closing workshop.
sources.limitations: No evaluation design, baseline or disaggregated beneficiary counts are provided; reported benefits are UNDP's summary, not independent impact estimates.

sources.title: Solomon Islands Advances National Climate Adaptation Planning
sources.organization: Solomon Islands Government, My SIG Services Portal
sources.temporal_coverage: NAP formulation workshop held 2026-10-20; CRVA and SIIVA assessment processes reported as current in October 2026.
sources.methodology: Government announcement summarizing the NAP workshop, the national Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment, and SIIVA work in two provinces.
sources.limitations: The announcement describes planning and assessment scope, not underlying CRVA or SIIVA findings or evaluated adaptation outcomes.

claims.locator: Printed p. 27, section 'Factors Outside the Control of Government', para. 94.
claims.paraphrase: The 2015-16 El Niño drought affected Central, Rennell and Bellona, and Temotu; schools closed and communities prioritized water projects.
institutions: Solomon Islands Ministry of Environment, Climate Change, Disaster Management and Meteorology
claims.limitations: The report attributes the drought to El Niño; this claim does not establish anthropogenic climate attribution.

claims.locator: Printed p. 14, para. 38 and Table 3 discussion.
claims.paraphrase: Over 80 percent of CRISP subprojects involved water, mainly rainwater harvesting; dry-season shortages made it a priority in Malaita, Rennell and Central.
claims.limitations: The ICR reports project outputs and stated priorities; it does not estimate comparative province-level water deficits.

claims.paraphrase: Sixty-three of 65 communities completed their highest-ranked climate-risk investment with PMU support; two completed their next priority because of cost constraints.
geographies: CRISP target communities across five provinces
claims.limitations: The aggregate result does not identify the two communities or establish long-term maintenance and resilience outcomes.

claims.locator: Printed p. 14, para. 40; printed p. 57, para. 16; Annex 8, printed p. 88.
claims.paraphrase: Tulagi's 260-metre shoreline works protected the road and foreshore trees during Tropical Cyclone Harold in April 2020.
claims.limitations: This is one completed project-site example, not a comparative or long-term evaluation of coastal protection.

claims.locator: Section 1.1, 'Overview: Rendova Island, Western Province, Solomon Islands.'
claims.paraphrase: Baniata had 533 residents and eight-community Lokuru had 1,065; households relied on gardens, fisheries, forest nuts and groundwater for food and livelihoods.

claims.locator: Section 3.1, 'Vulnerability assessment results – Baniata & Lokuru', Table 1.
claims.paraphrase: Both sites identified gardens, reefs and fish, water, rivers, shorelines and low-lying infrastructure as vulnerable; factors included hazard exposure, high dependence and weak resource management.
claims.limitations: Climate and non-climate drivers are combined; two pilot sites only.

claims.paraphrase: Workshops used local coordinators and women's and men's groups; priorities included leadership, health, farming, livelihood diversification, resource management and youth capacity.
claims.limitations: Priorities and plans; later implementation monitoring was still needed.

claims.paraphrase: Participants said cultural change and weaker local governance reduced use of traditional tabu areas; they proposed a community marine protected area and fisheries rules.
claims.limitations: Resource-governance finding, not a violent-conflict finding.

claims.locator: Section 2, 'Theoretical background', Honiara flood-displacement example; Section 3, methods, event ID 28 description.
claims.paraphrase: The authors describe an event in which people displaced by April 2014 floods to a Honiara informal settlement protested and rioted on 16 May, perceiving the government rehabilitation package as inadequate for their disaster losses.
claims.limitations: The article codes one event from news reports; it does not establish a general causal effect or climate-change attribution for the floods.
claims.source_stated_fcv_link: Authors link flood displacement to protest-turned-riot through grievances over perceived inadequate disaster rehabilitation.

claims.paraphrase: Across its Fiji, Solomon Islands and Vanuatu panel, the study found no statistically significant association between climate-related disasters or temperature extremes and social-conflict risk, including models separating protests and riots.
claims.limitations: The study covers 72 grid cells over 2012-2020; its null association does not rule out untested mechanisms, longer lags or future effects.

claims.locator: Article paragraphs on the programme's community outputs: West Kwarae, South Malaita, West Are'are and Afio Primary School.
claims.paraphrase: UNDP reports an expanded agroforestry nursery in West Kwarae, mangrove rehabilitation and a community centre in South Malaita, reforestation in West Are'are, and land restoration improving student access at Afio Primary School.
claims.limitations: The UNDP announcement summarizes project outputs without independent measurement of their durability or impact.

claims.locator: Article paragraph on the Marau Sound community project and paragraph on collective participation.
claims.paraphrase: UNDP reports that the Wahere Community Association built a seawall at Marau Sound, East Guadalcanal, to protect homes, infrastructure and livelihoods from coastal erosion and rising sea levels.
claims.limitations: The page gives no engineering assessment or quantified before-and-after exposure results.

claims.locator: Government announcement paragraphs on the CRVA, SIIVA, and the NAP formulation process.
claims.paraphrase: The government reports that the NAP was under formulation in October 2026, drawing on a 12-sector CRVA with consultations in all nine provinces and SIIVA assessments in Isabel and Makira focused on daily climate and livelihood effects.
systems: Solomon Islands Integrated Vulnerability and Adaptation Assessments
institutions: Ministry of Environment, Climate Change, Disaster Management and Meteorology
claims.limitations: The announcement gives assessment scope and planning status, not the underlying provincial findings or completed NAP actions.

claims.locator: Government announcement paragraphs on locally appropriate adaptation, customary land and participation in the NAP process.
claims.paraphrase: Government officials said the NAP should respect customary land arrangements and include women, young people, older people and persons with disabilities in adaptation planning.
claims.limitations: This is a stated planning commitment; the article does not verify participation or equitable outcomes.

search_audit.query: Solomon Islands subnational climate vulnerability named province community drought flood coastal erosion adaptation report primary source
search_audit.outcome: Found project-evaluation evidence for five CRISP provinces, original community research in Baniata and Lokuru on Rendova, and current government reporting on all-province CRVA consultations and SIIVA work in Isabel and Makira. A 2025 South Malaita ESRAM full report could not be opened.

search_audit.query: Solomon Islands climate conflict disaster displacement Honiara protest riot climate security primary research climate-conflict empirical study
search_audit.outcome: Found a 2026 original study describing a 2014 post-flood displacement and rehabilitation-grievance protest-turned-riot in Honiara, alongside a three-country panel finding no statistically significant overall disaster or temperature effect on social-conflict risk. The authors caution that the event mechanism is not directly tested statistically.

search_audit.query: Solomon Islands conflict insecurity disrupted climate adaptation project delivery reverse FCV adaptation access provincial report
search_audit.outcome: No inspected source established that insecurity or organized violence stopped a named climate-adaptation activity. The CRISP ICR documents logistics and delays from natural hazards, weather and COVID-19, not conflict; the Honiara event paper describes post-flood grievance rather than conflict constraining adaptation.

search_audit.query: Solomon Islands climate adaptation resilience community project evaluation local leadership women youth water food security named sites
search_audit.outcome: Found evaluated CRISP outputs in remote provinces, community-designed adaptation priorities and governance capacity in Rendova villages, and 2026 UNDP-reported community projects in Malaita and East Guadalcanal. UNDP's account is a completion announcement, not an independent evaluation.

gaps: The evidence is site- and project-specific; it does not provide a comprehensive current vulnerability ranking across provinces or province-level conflict incidence.

The 2026 climate-conflict study reports one Honiara post-flood protest-turned-riot but finds no statistically significant aggregate disaster or temperature effect for its three-country panel; the event mechanism was not statistically tested.

No source located in the targeted searches showed insecurity or organized violence interrupting a named climate-adaptation delivery operation; no such reverse pathway is inferred from historical unrest.

The CRISP ICR survey was non-representative and excluded Rennell and Bellona; the Western Province study purposively selected two communities and its adaptation-plan implementation required subsequent monitoring.

The 2026 CRVA story map did not render substantive text in direct access, the 2025 South Malaita ESRAM download failed, and the 2019 State of Environment PDF returned 403. Their findings are not used here.
